presentingComplaint: Persistent nagging cough for 10 days after a 'head cold', now bringing up discoloured phlegm
history: Retired schoolteacher, ex-smoker (quit 8 years ago, 15 pack-years) with no diagnosis of COPD or asthma and normal exercise tolerance until this illness. Ten days ago developed sore throat, blocked nose and generalised aches which settled within 4-5 days. However a dry cough that started with the coryza has persisted and become intermittently productive of yellow-green sputum over the last 3 days, worse at night and on talking, with occasional end-expiratory wheeze he can hear himself. He denies frank fevers, rigors, breathlessness at rest, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, weight loss or night sweats. No paroxysms of coughing, whoop or post-tussive vomiting. No recent travel, TB contact, aspiration risk or immunosuppression. This subtle, lingering post-viral picture without systemic toxicity is the atypical feature - it superficially raises concern for pneumonia or a COPD/asthma flare, but the trajectory and examination point to self-limiting acute bronchitis. He is anxious and specifically requesting antibiotics because the sputum is 'coloured'.
examination: Comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences, well perfused and not toxic. No accessory muscle use. Oropharynx unremarkable, no tonsillar exudate, no significant cervical lymphadenopathy. Chest: normal expansion and resonance; air entry good bilaterally with scattered high-pitched expiratory wheeze and a few coarse sounds that clear on coughing; NO focal crackles, NO bronchial breathing, NO area of dullness. Occasional cough during examination productive of mucopurulent sputum. Cardiovascular and abdominal examination normal. No peripheral oedema or clubbing.

labs.procalcitonin: 0.06 ng/mL (low - does not support bacterial infection)

imaging: Chest X-ray (PA): clear lung fields, no focal consolidation, effusion or cavitation; normal cardiac silhouette and hila. Effectively excludes pneumonia.
microbiology: Respiratory multiplex viral PCR positive for human rhinovirus/enterovirus. Sputum Gram stain and culture not indicated in uncomplicated acute bronchitis. Blood cultures not performed (no systemic sepsis).
differentialDiagnoses: Community-acquired pneumonia (excluded by clear CXR, no focal signs, normal vitals and low procalcitonin)
Acute exacerbation of COPD or asthma (no prior obstructive lung disease, isolated post-viral cough)
Upper respiratory tract infection / persistent post-viral cough
Pertussis (no paroxysms, whoop or post-tussive vomiting)
finalDiagnosis: Acute bronchitis (viral, post-coryzal) in an ex-smoker with subtle protracted cough and transient bronchial hyper-reactivity
citations: ACP/CDC - Appropriate Antibiotic Use for Acute Respiratory Tract Infection in Adults (Acute Bronchitis), 2016
CHEST (ACCP) - Diagnosis and Management of Cough: Acute Bronchitis, 2006
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Acute Bronchitis
stewardship: Uncomplicated acute bronchitis is predominantly viral and self-limiting - antibiotics are NOT indicated and do not shorten illness. Purulent/discoloured sputum reflects sloughed tracheobronchial epithelium and inflammatory cells, NOT bacterial infection, and must not trigger a prescription. Management is symptomatic (fluids, analgesia/antipyretics, honey, consideration of a short bronchodilator trial for the wheeze) with clear safety-netting: cough may persist up to 3 weeks. Antibiotics are reserved only for specific exceptions - suspected pertussis (macrolide), a superimposed COPD/CAP diagnosis, or frailty/high risk with deterioration. Low procalcitonin and a clear chest film support withholding antibiotics.
contraindications: Avoid empirical antibiotics for uncomplicated acute bronchitis (drives resistance, C. difficile, adverse effects with no benefit)
If a macrolide is ever used for suspected pertussis, review QT-prolonging drug interactions
Avoid sedating antitussives/codeine in the elderly or those at aspiration risk
edgeCases: Suspected pertussis: paroxysmal cough >2 weeks with whoop or post-tussive vomiting - then a macrolide (e.g. azithromycin/clarithromycin) IS indicated
Underlying COPD/asthma unmasking as an infective exacerbation would change management
Development of focal signs, hypoxia, high fever, tachypnea or a positive CXR reclassifies as pneumonia
Immunocompromise or frailty lowers the threshold for investigation and treatment
expectedMaiK: Recognise acute bronchitis as a self-limiting, predominantly viral lower respiratory infection; sputum discoloration/purulence does NOT indicate bacterial infection or justify antibiotics. Exclude pneumonia clinically (no focal crackles/bronchial breathing, normal vitals, no hypoxia/tachypnea, clear CXR) and then manage symptomatically with safety-netting rather than prescribing antibiotics.
expectedNextQuestions: Are there red flags for pneumonia (high fever, rigors, pleuritic pain, breathlessness, hypoxia)?
Any paroxysmal cough, whoop or post-tussive vomiting suggesting pertussis?
Known COPD, asthma or other chronic lung disease, and baseline exercise tolerance?
Smoking history, immunosuppression, or frailty/comorbidity that would alter risk?
Duration and trajectory of the cough - is it improving or worsening?
expectedInvestigations: Chest X-ray only if focal signs, abnormal vitals (tachypnea, hypoxia, tachycardia), high fever or diagnostic uncertainty, to exclude pneumonia
Procalcitonin/CRP optional to support withholding antibiotics
Pertussis testing if paroxysmal cough with characteristic features

investigations: Chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia if focal signs or abnormal vitals

regressionAssertions: Must diagnose ACUTE_BRONCHITIS and not escalate to CAP given clear CXR, no focal signs and normal vitals
Must NOT recommend antibiotics for uncomplicated acute bronchitis
Must not treat purulent/discoloured sputum as evidence of bacterial infection
Should recommend symptomatic management with safety-netting and pneumonia red-flag advice
